title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text: Analysis, October 2026. An analysis of the Claude Code team’s post Solving code review at Anthropic, read in the light of my earlier paper Intent Is the Source. Unless stated otherwise, numbers come from that post. Figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text:
The bottleneck moved
Once a team adopts agentic coding, code stops being the bottleneck. Review takes its place. PRs pile up, everyone is nervous to approve them, and the speed you gained writing code is lost waiting for someone to read it.



Figure 1. Schematic. When people write every line, writing is the slow step and review keeps up. When agents write, changes arrive in minutes and the queue forms in front of the reader.


The Claude Code team at Anthropic, where Claude writes roughly 90% of the code, recently shared how they handled this. Between June and September, their merged PRs more than doubled while the share of reverted PRs fell by over 40%. They did not remove review. They moved most of the reading to machines and pointed human attention at the risk.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text:
Six layers and a classifier
Their approach stacks six layers of checks with fast rollback underneath: verification, required CI, AI review, security review, human approval, and a merge queue with feature flags.



Figure 2. Schematic, my drawing of the setup described in the post. A change falls through six layers of checks, with fast rollback underneath. A risk classifier reads each change and decides how many people layer 5 needs.


A few principles hold it together:

Review happens before the PR exists. It runs continuously, more like a spellchecker than a gate at the end. By the time a human looks, Claude has usually reviewed and fixed the change at least once.
The agent must prove its work. Tests, a build, or a screenshot compared against the design. It shows output instead of claiming it is done, and a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context.
Risk is assessed per change. A classifier reads the change, not the author, and sets the tier. Low-risk changes merge without a human if automated review passes. Medium risk needs one person, high risk needs two.
Accountability stays human. Whoever prompted a change owns it and counts as a required reviewer. An agent’s approval never replaces a human one.
The reviewer keeps learning. Past incidents become daily evals, noise is measured by how people react to comments, and review rounds are capped so author and reviewer agents converge instead of looping.

It is a thoughtful system, and I largely agree with it.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text:
What the numbers show
The results are strong, but they come from one team measuring itself. Merged PRs can double because changes got smaller, so the count says more about pace than about how much was built. A revert is also only one measure of quality: a bug fixed forward, or switched off behind a flag, never shows up as a revert. What the numbers do show is the claim that matters most. The pace of merges rose sharply and quality, by this measure, improved.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text:
What review quietly did
PR review was never only about catching bugs. It also built a shared understanding of the codebase. Reading each other’s diffs is how teams learned the architecture, absorbed the conventions, and noticed when someone was drifting from them.
That side effect is now mostly gone. Anthropic writes that nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code, “and we don’t think anyone needs to.”
I half agree. Not everyone needs every detail. But the whole team should understand the main architectural patterns, the interfaces and the conventions. Open Slack channels and asking Claude to explain bits of code on demand are useful, but they are not the final answer.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
section: Let go of one more thing
text:
Let go of one more thing
Here is where I would push further. We need to let go of the belief that shared understanding has to come from reading code.
In practice, review served as an accidental knowledge channel. You learned the system as a by-product of checking someone else’s work. That worked when humans wrote every line at human speed. At agentic speed it cannot scale, and trying to preserve it is nostalgia.
We have done this before. Decades ago we stopped reading assembly, yet we still understood our systems, because understanding moved up a level of abstraction. Code is heading the same way.
The comparison has a limit, and it matters. We could stop reading assembly because compilers are deterministic: once we trusted one, it stayed trusted. Agents are not. In Intent Is the Source I called them stochastic compilers, correct only up to their checks. So this climb is safe only if the level above can be checked. Intent written only as prose would not be enough.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text:
The intent layer
Make shared understanding deliberate instead. Humans own the intent: architecture decisions, interface contracts, invariants and conventions. Agents own the implementation. Review checks one against the other.



Figure 3. Schematic. People own the top layer; each part lives in an artefact that agents can follow and reviewers can enforce. A change to the intent always goes to a person. The implementation below is large, changes fast and is read on demand. In an incident, someone still goes deep.


The intent layer becomes the artifact the team reads, discusses and evolves together. It is short enough that everyone can hold it in their head, and explicit enough that agents can follow it and reviewers can enforce it. Conventions live in agent instructions and linters. Contracts live in typed interfaces and tests. Decisions live in short records that explain the why.
This also tells us when a person must read. A change that only implements existing intent can be checked by machines: the tests pass, the contracts hold, the linters stay quiet. A change that alters the intent always goes to a person, whatever its size. That covers a new contract, a weakened invariant or a reversed decision. It also covers the most common quiet failure of coding agents: an agent that edits a test until it passes has changed the intent, not implemented it.
The same rule keeps the intent layer from drifting, the way design documents usually do. The code is checked against it on every change, and it cannot change unless someone decides it should. Not every part can be checked by a machine. Contracts, invariants and conventions can. Decisions are prose, so the AI reviewer and people check that a change still respects them. The rule fits the Anthropic setup well: their risk classifier could treat any change to the intent layer as high risk by definition.

title: Review the Intent, Not the Diff
text:
Where it breaks
Abstractions leak. When an incident hits, someone still has to go deep into the code. That skill fades when nobody uses it, so teams will need to keep it on purpose: incident drills, rotating who traces a bug by hand, reading the code behind a decision record from time to time.
Reading code does not go away. What goes away is the need to read all of it to know how the system works.
Own the why. Delegate the how. Review the intent, not the diff.

Read next · Intent Is the Source Why agentic coding is the next IDE and the next programming language.


The views in this analysis are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
Essay, October 2026. A companion to Fast AI, An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle and The Junior Colleague. All figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py. Where a figure uses someone else’s numbers, the caption names the source. Where the numbers are my own illustrative assumptions, the caption says so.
In short. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is usually presented as a way to give AI models access to tools. I think it does something larger. It changes what we mean by an API. A classic API is a contract that a developer reads once and then turns into code. An MCP server describes itself as data that any caller reads when it makes the call: what each tool does, what it accepts and returns, and whether it is safe to retry. The agentic loop is what made this practical, because for the first time a general client can read the description and act on it. But the idea does not need AI. A workflow engine, a form generator, a test suite or a policy gateway can read the same description. Once interfaces are data, tools can be connected as a graph of any shape, the same capability can be offered at several levels of detail, and much of the glue code between systems disappears. Pushed one step further, a tool can be found by the meaning of its description and can return not data but a program: a sub-graph of other tools, checked and run by an executor, then kept as a new tool. Programs then live inside the process, as data. MCP also has serious weaknesses: it fills the model’s context, it opens new security holes, and plain prose is a weak contract. Some of the alternatives are better for parts of the job. My conclusion is that the lasting change is not the protocol. It is the habit of publishing an interface as data and choosing, case by case, when to bind to it.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
1. The ritual of the SDK
Anyone who has connected two business systems knows the ritual. You find the documentation of the other system’s API. You read it, usually twice. You install its SDK for your language, or write a client if none exists. You map its objects to yours, handle its errors, its paging, its authentication, its rate limits. You write tests. Months later, the other side publishes version 3, and you start again.
The cost of this ritual is not in any single step. It is in the number of times we repeat it. Every pair of systems that must talk needs its own piece of glue, written by a person who has read the documentation of both. In a company with ten applications and fifty services, that is a lot of glue, and most of it does nothing more interesting than translate one shape of data into another.
For thirty years the answer has been better documentation and better code generation: WSDL in the early 2000s, then Swagger and OpenAPI, then typed client generators. They helped. But the contract was still read by a person and bound into code before the program ran. The program itself never knew what the service could do. It only knew what its developer had written down.

title: The Interface Is Data
section: 2. What MCP changes: the description is read at run time
text:
2. What MCP changes: the description is read at run time
MCP was published by Anthropic in November 2024 as an open standard for connecting AI applications to data and tools (Anthropic 2024). Technically it is modest. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0. A server exposes tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (reusable instructions). A client asks the server what it offers with tools/list and calls a tool with tools/call (Model Context Protocol 2025). The protocol says openly that it takes inspiration from the Language Server Protocol, which solved a similar problem between code editors and programming languages (Microsoft 2016).
What matters is in the answer to tools/list. Each tool comes back as a small piece of data: a name, a human-readable title, a description in plain words, a JSON Schema for its input, and since the June 2025 revision, an optional schema for its output and annotations: hints such as whether the tool only reads, whether it can destroy something, whether it is safe to call twice (Model Context Protocol 2025). The server can also tell the client that its list of tools has changed.



Figure 1. Schematic. With an SDK, a person reads the documentation and binds the interface into code, once per pair of systems. With described tools, the caller reads the interface as data when it makes the call.


None of these fields is new on its own. JSON Schema has existed for more than fifteen years, and OpenAPI already carries descriptions. The change is when the interface is bound, and by whom. With an SDK, the binding happens when the code is written, in the head of a developer. With MCP, it happens when the call is made, inside the caller. The program no longer contains the knowledge of what the service can do. It asks.



Figure 2. One entry of a tools/list answer, with the parts that different readers use. The fields follow the MCP specification (version 2025-06-18); the invoice tool is my own example.


This is why I say MCP is a way to redefine the API, at least in part. An API was a document plus a library. Here it becomes a data object that travels with the service, can be queried, filtered, logged, versioned and compared, like any other data.

title: The Interface Is Data
section: 3. An old dream, finally with a reader
text:
3. An old dream, finally with a reader
The dream of services that describe themselves is old, and it is worth remembering why it failed.
In 2000, Roy Fielding’s dissertation defined REST and one of its constraints, hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS): a client should discover what it can do next from the links in each response, not from documentation read in advance (Fielding 2000). Almost nobody built clients that way. Around the same time, WSDL described web services in machine-readable XML (Christensen et al. 2001), and UDDI registries were supposed to let programs find services on their own. The large public UDDI registries closed in 2006.
These ideas did not fail because they were wrong. They failed because the client was missing. A description is only useful if something can read it and decide what to do. A conventional program cannot read “assigns an invoice to a budget and to the person who approves it” and work out when to call it. So in practice a developer always read the description, and the binding stayed in the code.
The agentic loop supplied that client. A language model can read a description in plain words, match it to a goal, fill in the arguments from the schema, look at the result and decide what to do next (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023). Function calling, introduced by OpenAI in June 2023 (OpenAI 2023), gave models a structured way to do this, but each application still carried its own list of functions. Research on agents that choose among thousands of real APIs (Patil et al. 2023; Qin et al. 2024) showed both the promise and the difficulty. MCP’s contribution was to move the description out of the application and into the service, behind one protocol. Adoption was quick. By December 2025, when Anthropic gave MCP to the new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, it counted more than 10,000 active public MCP servers (Anthropic 2025b).

title: The Interface Is Data
section: 4. The idea does not need AI
text:
4. The idea does not need AI
This is the part I find most interesting, and most often missed. Once a service publishes its interface as data, the language model becomes just one of its readers.



Figure 3. Schematic. One tool description, six readers. Only the language model needs AI; the other five work from the same data with ordinary code.



A workflow engine or a plain script can call a tool by name, with arguments checked against the schema, and never involve a model.
A form generator can build a screen from the input schema, so a person can call the same tool by hand.
A test generator can produce valid and invalid calls from the schemas and check that the outputs match the output schema.
A policy gateway can read the annotations and decide, for example, that destructive tools require a human approval.
A catalogue can index every tool in the company, with its owner, its version and how often it is used.

Seen this way, MCP is less an AI protocol than a data-driven way of building integrations. The interface is a record in a catalogue. The behaviour of the system, which tools exist, who may call them, which ones chain together, can be changed by changing data rather than code. The agentic loop is optional. The description is not.
This matters for the argument I made in Fast AI. There I argued that the large model should do the slow, exploratory work once, and that what repeats should be compiled into something fast and fixed. A data-driven interface makes that compilation easy: the recipe an agent discovered can be stored as data (call extract_invoice, then match_po, then pick_approver) and replayed by a workflow engine with no model at all.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
5. A web of tools
The second consequence is structural. In MCP, the roles of client and server are not fixed: a server can itself be a client of other servers. An “invoice desk” server can expose a single tool, route_invoice, and implement it by calling an ERP server, a document server and a decision model. A gateway can collect many servers behind one catalogue and add identity, policy and logging in one place.



Figure 4. The arithmetic of glue. With one adapter per pair, the work grows as N \times M; with one adapter per side, as N + M. Plain counting, not a measurement.


The first gain is simple arithmetic, the same one that motivated the Language Server Protocol. If N clients must each talk to M services, writing one adapter per pair costs N \times M adapters. If every client speaks one protocol and every service publishes one description, it costs N + M. With ten clients and fifty services, that is 60 adapters instead of 500. Each adapter is real work: reading, coding, testing, and above all maintaining it when either side changes. I suspect this, more than anything AI-related, is where most of the time is saved.



Figure 5. Schematic. A web of tools. Clients, with or without a model, reach servers through a gateway. The invoice desk is both a server and a client. The dashed green links are not configured by hand: they can be computed by matching one tool’s output schema to another tool’s input schema.


The second gain is less obvious. When every tool declares the shape of what it accepts and returns, the connections between tools become something you can compute. If extract_invoice returns an object that fits the input of match_po, the two can be chained, and a planner, human or machine, can see this without reading any code. The graph of possible compositions is a by-product of the descriptions. This is what I mean by a web of tools: not a fixed integration diagram drawn by an architect, but a graph that can be queried, searched for paths, and checked for missing links.



Figure 6. Schematic. The same tools, arranged in three shapes. Because every node speaks the same protocol, the shape is a deployment choice, not a rewrite.


And the graph can take whatever shape the organisation needs. A hub puts identity and policy in one place, which most companies will want for anything that touches money or personal data. A mesh lets teams connect their servers directly, with no central bottleneck. Layers stack atomic tools under composite tools, and composite tools under agents that are themselves exposed as tools. Because every node speaks the same protocol, moving from one shape to another is a matter of configuration. This is the cross-communication benefit: teams that never coordinated their APIs can still find and call each other’s tools, through one catalogue, in one format.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
6. Granularity on demand
Every API designer faces the question of grain. Too fine, and callers make dozens of chatty calls to do one thing. Too coarse, and callers cannot do anything the designer did not foresee. In the SDK world, the designer picks one grain and everybody lives with it.
Described tools loosen this choice in two ways.



Figure 7. Schematic. One capability offered at four grains, from an agent used as a single tool down to the raw operations underneath. Each caller picks the level it needs.


First, the same server can publish several levels at once. At the top, a whole capability exposed as one tool: “handle this invoice task”, implemented by an agent. Below it, a few workflows that each deliver one result. Below those, single actions. At the bottom, the raw operations of the underlying API. A strong model working on an unusual case may want the fine tools. A workflow engine wants the workflow. Another team’s agent may only want the capability. Because each level is just more data in the same catalogue, offering all four costs little. Anthropic’s advice on writing tools for agents points the same way: fewer, more meaningful tools that match how a task is really done, rather than a thin wrapper around every endpoint (Anthropic 2025e).
Second, the caller can choose how much of the description to read. This is progressive disclosure: first the names, then the descriptions of the tools that look relevant, then their full schemas, then, if needed, their documentation or code. Agent Skills apply this idea to instructions: a model sees only a skill’s name and summary until it decides the skill is relevant, and only then reads the rest (Anthropic 2025c). Tool search does the same for large tool catalogues: tools are loaded only when a search finds them (Anthropic 2025d; Gan and Sun 2025).



Figure 8. What a caller reads before it acts. Left: a catalogue of 200 tools, assuming about 10 tokens per name, 50 per name and description, and 450 per full schema; my own illustrative values. Right: one workflow reported by Anthropic, where presenting tools as files read on demand reduced the tokens used from 150,000 to 2,000 (Anthropic 2025a).


The numbers show why this matters. Loading every schema of a large catalogue before the first call can cost tens of thousands of tokens, which are paid on every run and push useful context out of the window. In one workflow described by Anthropic, presenting the tools as files that the agent reads only when needed reduced the tokens used from 150,000 to 2,000, a reduction of 98.7% (Anthropic 2025a). That is one example, not a benchmark, but the direction is clear: granularity is no longer only a property of the API. It is a choice made by the caller, at run time, based on what it needs.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
7. Tools that return programs
So far, every tool in this essay has returned data. I want to push the idea one step further, because I think this is where the paradigm becomes really new: a tool can return a program, and that program can stay inside the process as data.

7.1 A catalogue you search by meaning
If a tool’s description is data, it can be embedded: turned into a vector by the same kind of model used for semantic search (Reimers and Gurevych 2019). The catalogue then becomes a space in which tools that do similar things sit close together. A question, from a person, an agent or another tool, lands somewhere in that space, and its nearest neighbours are the few tools worth reading.



Figure 9. Schematic, with hand-placed positions. Tool descriptions as points in a space of meaning, grouped by what they do. A question is embedded in the same space; its five nearest tools are returned, and only their schemas are read.


None of this is speculative. ToolLLM and Gorilla used a retriever to pick a handful of APIs out of thousands (Qin et al. 2024; Patil et al. 2023), and the tool search in current agent platforms works the same way (Anthropic 2025d; Gan and Sun 2025). ToolkenGPT goes further and gives each tool its own token embedding inside the model, so that calling a tool is no different from predicting a word (Hao et al. 2023).
Embeddings give the web of §5 a second kind of edge. Schema edges say which tools can be chained, because one’s output fits another’s input. Embedding distance says which tools are about the same thing. Together they are enough to propose a plan without anyone drawing it.


7.2 A tool whose result is a sub-graph
Now the step that interests me most. Nothing in the idea of a tool requires its result to be plain data. A tool can return a small graph of other tool calls, with the arguments of each node wired to the outputs of the others.



Figure 10. Schematic. A tool whose result is a program. plan_invoice_routing does not route the invoice; it returns a graph of five tool calls. An executor checks the graph and runs it, in parallel where the dependencies allow, without a model. The "returns": "graph" format is my own convention; MCP does not define one.


In Figure 10, plan_invoice_routing does not do the work. It returns the recipe: extract the invoice; then, in parallel, match the purchase order and fetch the supplier’s rules; then pick the approver; then notify them. An executor, which is ordinary code, checks the graph before running anything: every tool exists, every reference fits the schema it feeds, there is no cycle, the policy gateway accepts every node, and the whole stays within its limits. Then it runs the graph, with no model in the loop.
Research on agents points the same way. ReWOO separates planning from execution: the model writes the whole plan once, instead of reasoning again after every observation (Xu et al. 2023). LLMCompiler has the model emit a graph of function calls with their dependencies and runs the independent calls in parallel, which made runs faster and cheaper than step-by-step reasoning (Kim et al. 2024). Code mode and programmatic tool calling let the model write the plan as code (Varda and Pai 2025; Anthropic 2025d).
What changes in my proposal is who returns the plan. It need not be the model in the loop. It can be a tool like any other: written by a team, generated by a model and reviewed once, or retrieved from storage. The plan stops being a private thought of the agent and becomes part of the interface.


7.3 Programs inside programs
Since a node of a returned graph is just a tool call, it can itself be a tool that returns a graph.



Figure 11. Schematic. Programs nest. The process calls route_invoice, which returns a graph of four steps; one of them, approve, returns a graph of its own. The executor expands each level only when it is reached, within a maximum depth and a budget of calls.


This gives the multiple levels of detail of §6 almost for free. Nobody has to design the levels in advance: each one expands only when it is reached, and only as far as needed. A caller that trusts route_invoice treats it as one step. A caller that must audit it can ask for the graph and inspect every level. The executor needs two limits to make sure the expansion ends: a maximum depth and a budget of calls.


7.4 Keeping the programs
The last step closes the loop with Fast AI. A returned graph is data. It can be logged, compared with yesterday’s, reviewed by a person, signed, versioned and stored. Once stored with a description, it is itself a tool: it gets embedded in the same catalogue, and the next search for “who must approve this supplier invoice?” finds the stored program before anything has to plan.



Figure 12. Schematic. Programs inside the process. Search finds the tools, a planner returns a sub-graph, the executor checks it and runs it, and the graph is kept. Published back as a tool, it is found first the next time, and planning is skipped.


Voyager, an agent that played Minecraft, worked this way: it stored every skill it learned as a program, indexed it by an embedding of its description, retrieved it when a similar task came up, and built new skills from old ones (Wang et al. 2023). Models that write their own tools and reuse them follow the same pattern (Cai et al. 2024).
In a company, the same mechanism means that the programs which run the business live inside the process, as data you can inspect, rather than hidden in the code of each application or worked out again by an agent every morning. This is what I mean by embedding programs in the process. The process is a graph of tools. Some tools return graphs. Those graphs can be kept and become tools. The difference between an API, a workflow and a program becomes a matter of level, not of kind. Programmers will recognise an old idea from Lisp, where code and data share one form. Here, the shared form is the tool description.


7.5 What it costs
A tool that returns a program is a tool that returns code, and everything §8.1 says about poisoned descriptions applies with more force. The executor must treat every returned graph as untrusted. It should run only tools from an allowed list, check every reference against its schema, apply the policy to every node and not only to the first, enforce the limits, and never let a graph call a tool its caller could not call directly. Debugging is harder too: a failure can sit three levels down, in a graph nobody wrote by hand, so every expansion must be logged with where it came from. Finally, there is no standard. MCP has no “graph” result type, so today this is a convention on top of the protocol, or a job for a workflow engine. A shared format for returned plans would, I think, be one of the most useful next steps for the ecosystem.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
8. The case against MCP
So far I have made the case for. It would be dishonest to stop there. MCP has drawn serious criticism, much of it fair, and for several jobs there are better options.

8.1 Five objections
It is a wrapper over APIs that already exist. Many MCP servers are thin layers over a REST API that already had an OpenAPI description. Adding a protocol, a server process and a new failure point to say the same thing again is not obviously progress. Critics argue that a model that can read OpenAPI, or a --help page, does not need MCP at all (Ronacher 2025).
It crowds the model’s context. Every tool description an agent loads costs tokens on every call, and accuracy in choosing the right tool falls as the list grows (Gan and Sun 2025). In the paper I analysed in The Junior Colleague, each task offered 68 tools, 31 of them near-duplicates of the core ones, precisely because large, messy catalogues are what agents face in practice (Zhu et al. 2026). Progressive disclosure helps, but it is extra machinery that the protocol did not originally provide.
It opens new security holes. A tool description is text that the model reads and trusts. A malicious or compromised server can hide instructions in it, a tool-poisoning attack (Invariant Labs 2025). Any tool that returns content from the outside world can carry an indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023). Simon Willison named the dangerous combination the lethal trifecta: an agent with access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out (Willison 2025). Connecting many MCP servers to one agent makes that combination easy to assemble by accident. Surveys of the MCP ecosystem list these and other threats, such as name collisions between servers and installers that cannot be verified (Hou et al. 2025). The specification itself warns that annotations are hints and should not be trusted from an unknown server (Model Context Protocol 2025).
Prose is a weak contract. A schema says that amount_chf is a number. It does not say whether it includes VAT, whether calling the tool twice creates two approvals, or what happens if the budget is closed. A typed SDK does not say this either, but it is usually paired with a developer who read the documentation and wrote tests. When the reader is a model, the description is the documentation, and its gaps become errors at run time instead of questions at design time. Versioning is also weaker: a server can change its tools between two calls.
It is slower and less predictable than a function call. An agent that reads descriptions, reasons and then calls is orders of magnitude slower and more expensive than compiled code calling a library, and it may take a different path on the same input. For processes that run ten thousand times a day, this is the wrong trade, as I argued in Fast AI.


8.2 The alternatives



Figure 13. My own placement of the main ways to connect a caller to a service: when the interface is bound, and who reads it. Approaches in green were designed with agents in mind.



OpenAPI plus function calling. If a service already has a good OpenAPI description, it can be turned into function definitions for a model with no new protocol (OpenAPI Initiative 2021; OpenAI 2023). This keeps one source of truth and the existing tooling for authentication, gateways and testing.
Code as the interface. Instead of asking the model to call tools one at a time, let it write a short program against a typed API and run it in a sandbox. Research found that agents acting through code solved more tasks than agents emitting JSON calls (Wang et al. 2024). Cloudflare’s Code Mode turns MCP tools into a TypeScript API for exactly this reason (Varda and Pai 2025), and Anthropic’s code-execution approach does the same with files (Anthropic 2025a). In this view, the SDK comes back, but its reader is now a model.
Command-line tools and skills. A well-made CLI already describes itself through --help, composes through pipes, and is something models have seen countless times in training. Paired with short instruction files that are read on demand (Anthropic 2025c), it covers much of what developers use MCP for, with no server to run (Ronacher 2025).
Agent-to-agent protocols. When the thing on the other side is itself an agent with its own judgement, a protocol for tasks between peers, such as Google’s A2A, fits better than a list of tools (Google 2025; Ehtesham et al. 2025).
Typed SDKs and RPC. For hot paths, nothing beats a compiled call with types checked before the program runs.
GraphQL. Its introspection already lets a client ask what a service offers and choose exactly the fields it needs (GraphQL Foundation 2021). It solved part of the granularity problem years ago, for data.



8.3 My reading
Most of these alternatives share MCP’s core idea: the interface is described in a form the caller reads, and the binding happens later than it used to. Code mode reads MCP descriptions and generates an SDK from them. Skills are descriptions in files. A2A publishes “agent cards”. Even the critics who say “just use the CLI” are relying on --help, a self-description read at run time.
So I do not think the lasting change is MCP the wire format. It may be replaced, merged with other protocols, or survive mainly as an internal standard behind gateways. The lasting change is the practice: publish every interface as data, rich enough for a model and precise enough for a machine, and let each caller decide when to bind to it. MCP is, for now, the most widely adopted way to do that, and its governance under a neutral foundation makes it a reasonable bet. But the objections in §8.1 are about real costs, and the right answer to several of them is to use something else for that part of the job.

title: The Interface Is Data
text:
9. Where the SDK survives
Back to the original question: does this redefine the API and the SDK “to an extent” or “completely”? My answer is: completely at the edges, not in the core.



Figure 14. Schematic, with example tasks of my own. Where each kind of binding belongs, by how often the same call is made and how much the task varies. What an agent discovers in the upper left should be compiled into the lower right once it repeats.


At the edges, where integration happens, where a call is made rarely or differs every time, where a team needs to find and use another team’s capability, the described interface wins. It is cheaper to build, easier to discover and works for model and script alike. Here I expect hand-written SDKs to become rare.
In the core, where the same call runs thousands of times a day, the binding should happen early again: a typed client, a fixed recipe, a small decision model like the one in The Junior Colleague. The difference from before is where that code comes from. It does not need to start from a developer reading documentation. It can be generated from the same descriptions, or compiled from a path that an agent found and that people reviewed. The SDK becomes an output of the described interface, not its source.

title: The Interface Is Data
The Interface Is Data
text:
11. Conclusion
For decades, an API was a promise written for people. A developer read it, understood it, and turned it into code that was frozen until the next release. MCP and the agentic loop make a different arrangement possible: the promise is written as data, travels with the service, and is read by whoever calls it, at the moment of the call.
That one shift has several consequences. The caller no longer needs AI to benefit. Tools can be connected into a web of whatever shape suits the organisation, with far less glue. The same capability can be offered at several levels of detail, and each caller chooses how much to read. Tools can be found by meaning, and can return programs that are checked, run and kept as new tools, so the logic of a process lives inside it as data. And the expensive, exploratory work of figuring out how to combine tools can be done once by an agent, then compiled into something fast.
MCP may not be the protocol we use in ten years. Its weaknesses are real, and some of its alternatives are better at parts of the job. But I think the habit it is spreading will remain: an interface is not only something we read. It is data.

Read next · Fast AI Why the large model should build the memory once, instead of reasoning through every run.


The views in this essay are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
Essay, October 2026. A companion to Fast AI. All figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py. Where a figure or a sentence uses numbers from someone else’s work, the source is cited next to it and listed in the references. Where numbers are my own illustrative assumptions, the caption says so.
In short. I believe the future of AI is, to a large extent, local. But when people talk about local AI, they usually picture one big model made small enough to fit on a laptop. I see it differently: many specialised models, a memory they share, a thin harness around them, and a careful loop that lets them keep learning from the work they do. I have four reasons. The architectures of today’s largest models already moved in this direction. Simple arithmetic about memory and bandwidth favours it on a local machine. A thin harness can help small models where it no longer helps large ones. And our own brain most likely works this way: a huge set of specialised parts, a fast memory, a slow learner, and plasticity everywhere.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
1. The wrong picture
Models are getting smaller for the same capability. Xiao and colleagues measured this as capability density, and found that for open models it doubled roughly every three to three and a half months between 2023 and 2025 (Xiao et al. 2024). Better training, better architectures, quantisation and better chips all push in the same direction. I am convinced a large part of AI will move closer to where the work happens: onto our laptops, phones, machines and private servers.
But the picture most of us have in mind is one giant brain, waiting to be compressed into a smaller box. The question becomes “how much of the big model can I run locally?”, and the answer is always “a bit less than you would like, but wait a year.”
I would rather ask a different question: what would intelligence look like if it were designed for the machine in front of me from the start?



Figure 1. Two ways to organise intelligence. An oracle sends every task to one large model. An ecosystem sends each task to a small specialist, chosen by a router, and all specialists share one memory. Schematic, my own.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
section: 2. What I mean by an ecosystem
text:
2. What I mean by an ecosystem
By an ecosystem, I mean five parts working together on one machine:

Specialists. Small models, or adapters on a shared base model, each good at one job: reading invoices, writing queries, transcribing speech, a company’s own domain.
A router. A small model that decides which specialist handles a task, and when to escalate.
A shared memory. Knowledge and episodes stored outside the weights, readable and correctable by people.
A thin harness. The tools, checks and permissions around the models: run the tests, validate the output, keep the data local.
A consolidation loop. A slow process, for example at night, that turns verified experience into small, tested updates of the specialists.

A frontier model can stay outside, as a teacher and an occasional consultant.



Figure 2. The local ecosystem I have in mind. A router sends each task to a specialist. Specialists read from and write to a shared memory. At night, the system consolidates what it has learned into updated specialists. A frontier model, outside the machine, teaches once and is consulted rarely. Schematic, my own.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
section: 3. Today’s largest models already point this way
text:
3. Today’s largest models already point this way
From dense to mixtures of experts. A classic language model is dense: to produce each word, it uses every one of its parameters. Many of today’s largest models are mixtures of experts instead. The idea goes back to Shazeer and colleagues (Shazeer et al. 2017) and was scaled up in the Switch Transformer (Fedus et al. 2022). Inside, the model is split into many sub-networks, and for each word a small gate chooses a few of them.
Two published examples make the point:

Mixtral 8x7B has 46.7 billion parameters, but each word uses about 12.9 billion: two of its eight experts per layer (Jiang et al. 2024).
DeepSeek-V3 has 671 billion parameters, but each word uses about 37 billion (DeepSeek-AI 2024). Its design is telling: in each expert layer, one shared expert is used for every word, and 8 of 256 routed experts are chosen for that word. A common core, plus specialists picked on demand.




Figure 3. Three architectures. A dense model loads all its parameters and uses all of them for every word. A mixture of experts loads all of them but uses only a few experts per word. An ecosystem loads separate specialist models when they are needed. Schematic, my own.





Figure 4. Share of parameters used for each word. Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 values are computed from the published parameter counts (Jiang et al. 2024; DeepSeek-AI 2024). The cortex value is a rough estimate of the share of neurons that can be strongly active at the same time, from energy constraints (Lennie 2003); it is debated and shown hatched. Chart my own.


The people who build the largest models have concluded that not everything should work on everything. But a mixture of experts is still one model. All its experts must be loaded in memory, even if only a few work at a time. They are trained together, so you cannot replace one without touching the others. And they are not specialists a person would recognise: an expert is a part of the network that training happened to route certain words to.
The other pieces already exist too. What I call an ecosystem is mostly an assembly of things that already work:

Shared base plus adapters, in production. Apple’s on-device model has about 3 billion parameters and uses small, task-specific LoRA adapters that are swapped in for each task; a rank-16 adapter takes tens of megabytes (Gunter et al. 2024; Hu et al. 2022).
Many adapters on one machine. S-LoRA showed how to serve thousands of adapters on top of one base model (Sheng et al. 2023).
Experts trained separately. Branch-Train-MiX trains domain experts in parallel from a common starting model, then combines them (Sukhbaatar et al. 2024).
Routing between models. RouteLLM learns when a query can go to a cheaper model, and reports cost reductions of more than two times on some benchmarks without a loss in quality (Ong et al. 2025). FrugalGPT reports matching the best single model with large cost savings by cascading models (Chen et al. 2023).
Memory outside the weights. RETRO, with retrieval from a large text database, performs comparably to GPT-3 on the Pile benchmark with about 25 times fewer parameters (Borgeaud et al. 2022; Lewis et al. 2020).

None of these is the whole ecosystem. Together, they show that each part is not speculation. Researchers at NVIDIA recently made a similar case for agents: most of what agents do is a small number of repetitive, specialised tasks, which small models can handle more economically, with larger models called only when needed (Belcak et al. 2025).

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
section: 4. The arithmetic of a laptop: bandwidth
text:
4. The arithmetic of a laptop: bandwidth
This is the argument I find most convincing, because it is simple arithmetic.
When a model generates text for one person, each new word requires reading all the active weights from memory once, and doing roughly two operations per weight. With weights stored at b bits, a model with N_{\text{active}} active parameters reads N_{\text{active}} \cdot b/8 bytes per word. The speed is therefore bounded by the memory bandwidth B:

\text{words per second} \;\le\; \frac{B}{N_{\text{active}} \cdot b/8}.

Is bandwidth really the limit, and not computation? The roofline model answers this by comparing operations per byte (Williams et al. 2009). Decoding for one user at 4 bits does about two operations per half byte, so about 4 operations per byte read. A laptop GPU that can do tens of trillions of operations per second, with a bandwidth of about 500 GB/s, needs tens of operations per byte to be kept busy. Decoding offers far fewer, so it waits for memory.
Take a laptop with 128 GB of memory and up to 546 GB/s of bandwidth, the published figures for Apple’s M4 Max (Apple 2024). I use 500 GB/s and 4-bit weights:

Figure 5. Upper bound on generation speed when every word requires reading all active weights once, at 500 GB/s and 4-bit weights. Open circle: does not fit in 128 GB. Real speeds are lower; computation, the conversation’s cache and software all cost something. My own calculation from the formula above; DeepSeek-V3 parameter counts from (DeepSeek-AI 2024).


Two consequences follow. The same 128 GB that cannot hold one frontier model can hold about thirty 8-billion-parameter specialists, each of them fast. And this wall is not going away soon: over two decades, peak compute of server hardware grew about 3.0 times every two years, but memory bandwidth only about 1.6 times (Gholami et al. 2024). Techniques such as speculative decoding (Leviathan et al. 2023) help, but they help small models just as much as large ones.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
section: 5. The arithmetic of capacity: why specialists can be small
text:
5. The arithmetic of capacity: why specialists can be small
The second argument is about where a model spends its capacity.
Michaud and colleagues proposed a useful way to think about scaling: knowledge comes in discrete units, which they call quanta, used with very different frequencies, and a model learns them roughly in order of how often they are needed (Michaud et al. 2023). Here is a simple consequence, in my own words and with my own simplifications.
Suppose a task needs two kinds of quanta: a shared core (language, basic reasoning), which takes N_{\text{shared}} parameters, and domain knowledge, which takes N_{\text{domain}}. A specialist needs both:

N_{\text{specialist}} \approx N_{\text{shared}} + N_{\text{domain}}.

A general model is trained on everything, and the domain is only a share f of what it sees. In the simplest symmetric case, where many domains each have a share f and similar structure, the general model reaches the same depth in this domain only when it has learned as deep into every other domain too:

N_{\text{general}} \approx N_{\text{shared}} + \frac{N_{\text{domain}}}{f}.

With illustrative values of 2 billion for the core and 1 billion for the domain, a domain that is 1% of the general model’s training needs about 102 billion parameters for the same depth, against 3 billion for the specialist.



Figure 6. A simple capacity model. Parameters needed for the same depth in one domain, for a general model and for a specialist, as a function of the domain’s share f of the general model’s training. Illustrative values, my own: N_{\text{shared}} = 2B, N_{\text{domain}} = 1B, no transfer between domains beyond the shared core. Model inspired by the quanta view of scaling (Michaud et al. 2023).


The model is crude, and its main assumption, that domains do not help each other beyond the shared core, is not fully true. Knowledge does transfer between domains, and a general model like GPT-4, carefully prompted, has outperformed specialist medical models on medical benchmarks (Nori et al. 2023). That is exactly why the formula keeps N_{\text{shared}}: a good specialist is not trained from scratch, it starts from a strong shared core.
The published evidence is consistent with the direction of the argument. A 770-million-parameter model trained with explanations from a much larger model outperformed few-shot prompted 540-billion-parameter PaLM on a benchmark, using only 80% of the training data (Hsieh et al. 2023). A 1.3-billion-parameter model trained on carefully chosen data reached 50.6% on the HumanEval coding benchmark (Gunasekar et al. 2023). Narrow, well-taught models can be very small.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
section: 6. The arithmetic of many specialists: adapters
text:
6. The arithmetic of many specialists: adapters
If every specialist were a separate model, memory would fill up quickly. Adapters solve much of this.
A LoRA adapter replaces the update of a weight matrix of size d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}} by two thin matrices of rank r (Hu et al. 2022). Its size relative to the matrix is

\frac{r\,(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})}{d_{\text{in}}\,d_{\text{out}}} \;\approx\; \frac{2r}{d} \quad \text{for a square matrix}.

With r = 16 and d = 3072, that is about 1%. Applied to a 3-billion-parameter base model, an adapter has roughly 30 million parameters, about 60 MB at 16 bits, consistent with the “tens of megabytes” Apple reports for its rank-16 adapters (Gunter et al. 2024).



Figure 7. Memory needed for k specialists, as separate 3B models at 4 bits, or as one 3B base at 4 bits plus rank-16 adapters at 16 bits (about 60 MB each). My own calculation from the formula above.


One hundred specialists as adapters take about 7.5 GB; as separate models, 150 GB. There is a trade-off, and it is worth knowing: adapters learn less than full fine-tuning, but they also forget less of what the base model knew (Biderman et al. 2024). For a system that must keep learning without breaking, forgetting less is a feature.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
7. The arithmetic of routing
An ecosystem is only as good as its router. A simple model makes this precise.
Let a be the router’s accuracy, q_s the quality when a task reaches the right specialist, and q_w the quality when it reaches the wrong one. The expected quality is

q = a\,q_s + (1-a)\,q_w.

The ecosystem beats one general model of quality q_g that runs at a similar speed only if

a \;>\; a^{*} = \frac{q_g - q_w}{q_s - q_w}.

With illustrative values q_s = 0.90, q_w = 0.30 and q_g = 0.80, the router must be right more than 83% of the time. If the router also knows when it is unsure, and sends half of its mistakes to a larger model with quality q_L = 0.95, the threshold drops to about 64%.



Figure 8. Expected quality of an ecosystem as a function of router accuracy, with and without escalation of uncertain cases, compared to one general model that runs at a similar speed. Illustrative values, my own.


The lesson is not the exact numbers, which are mine. It is the shape: a router that knows its own uncertainty is worth more than a slightly better specialist. This is also what makes published routing work encouraging (Ong et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2023).

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
section: 8. The harness: thin around strong models, essential around small ones
text:
8. The harness: thin around strong models, essential around small ones
A recent study from EPFL and Apple asks how much of a harness (the orchestrators, sub-agents and retrieval layers built around a model) a strong agent needs for machine-learning engineering tasks. Under an equal time budget and the same frontier model, the elaborate open-source harnesses they tested gave no advantage over a single session of a minimal coding agent with direct access to read, write and run commands (Brilliantov et al. 2026). Their conclusion is that the model is the main driver of performance, and that elaborate harnesses around strong models give poor returns on current benchmarks.
At first sight, this goes against an ecosystem. If structure around a model does not help, why build an ecosystem at all? I read it differently, for three reasons.
First, it is a result about strong models. The study holds the frontier model fixed. It says that a strong model has absorbed much of what the scaffolding was doing. That fits Sutton’s “bitter lesson”: general methods that use more computation tend to beat hand-built structure in the long run (Sutton 2019). It says much less about a 3-billion-parameter model on a laptop.
Second, small models gain the most from the right kind of harness. Several results point that way:

The design of the interface matters: SWE-agent showed that giving a model well-designed commands to view, edit and test code improved results on software tasks, without changing the model (Yang et al. 2024).
A verifier turns attempts into results: with repeated attempts checked by the project’s own tests, an open model went from solving 15.9% of SWE-bench Lite issues in one attempt to 56% in 250 attempts, above the best single attempt reported at the time, 43% (Brown et al. 2024).
Extra computation at the time of answering, used well, allowed a smaller model to outperform a 14 times larger one, on problems where the smaller model already had a reasonable success rate (Snell et al. 2025).
Apple’s framework for its on-device model offers guided generation and constrained tool calling, which keep a small model’s output within a valid structure (Apple 2025).




Figure 9. Repeated attempts with a verifier. The two points are results reported by Brown et al. for SWE-bench Lite (Brown et al. 2024). The dashed line is my own calculation of what would happen if attempts were independent, 1-(1-p)^k with p = 0.159; the gap shows that attempts are strongly correlated. Chart my own.


The arithmetic is worth a sentence. If a single attempt succeeds with probability p and attempts were independent, k attempts would succeed with probability 1-(1-p)^k. In practice attempts are correlated, so the real gain is smaller, as the figure shows. But on a local machine, where a small specialist is fast and a test can check each answer, a few extra attempts cost very little.
Third, some of the harness can never be absorbed into a model. A persistent memory that lasts beyond one conversation. Permissions over what may leave the machine. Tests that decide whether an output or an update is accepted. The local data itself. However strong models become, these stay outside.



Figure 10. My own view of the harness, as a schematic. Scaffolding for reasoning (orchestrators, sub-agents, retries) adds much to small models and little to strong ones. Structure no model can absorb (memory, permissions, tests, local data) keeps its value. The right end is consistent with the finding of (Brilliantov et al. 2026); the rest of the curve is my hypothesis, not data.


So my conclusion is a design rule: keep the harness thin, and keep only what earns its place. Scaffolding that compensates for weak reasoning should be removable, and removed as specialists get better. Structure that gives memory, verification and control should stay.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
9. Our own brain
The last reason is closer to home. When I look at how our brain seems to be organised, it does not look like one dense model. It looks much more like an ecosystem. I want to be careful here, because biology does not prove anything about software, and the brain is not a set of neat boxes.
Many specialised parts. Neuroscience has found areas that respond to specific things. A classic example is an area of the visual cortex that responds much more strongly to faces than to other objects (Kanwisher et al. 1997). Damage to such areas can remove one ability and leave others almost intact. At the same time, representations are also distributed and overlapping across areas (Haxby et al. 2001). Specialised, but heavily connected.
Language and thinking are handled by different networks. One of the most striking recent results for my argument comes from the study of language. Brain imaging reliably finds a network that is engaged when we read or listen to sentences, and it is largely not engaged when we solve problems or reason; people who lose language through brain damage can still reason (Fedorenko et al. 2024). Mahowald and colleagues drew the consequence for AI: large language models are very good at the form of language, but their ability to reason and use it in the world is uneven, and models that work like humans may need separate mechanisms for the two (Mahowald et al. 2024).
And a general-purpose network, too. The brain is not only specialists. A multiple-demand network, spread over frontal and parietal areas, is engaged by many different demanding tasks and seems to help assemble the right parts for the problem at hand (Duncan et al. 2020). In the ecosystem, that is the role of the shared core and the router: one general part that coordinates many specialised ones.
Specialisation may simply be efficient. A recent experiment makes this more than an analogy. Dobs and colleagues trained artificial neural networks to recognise both faces and objects. Without being told to, the networks split themselves into separate systems for faces and for objects, much as the brain does (Dobs et al. 2022). Their interpretation is that specialisation is what good optimisation tends to produce when tasks are different enough.
Probably a very large number of units. Mountcastle proposed that the cortex is built from a repeated basic unit, the cortical column (Mountcastle 1997). Hawkins goes further and suggests that each column builds its own model of the world, and that they reach decisions together (Hawkins 2021); his team has since started an open project that builds AI from many such repeated learning modules (Clay et al. 2024). This is a theory, and it is debated. But the picture of a large number of similar units, each specialised by what it receives, is widely shared.
A fast memory and a slow learner. The theory of complementary learning systems proposes that the hippocampus learns new episodes quickly, while the neocortex learns slowly, by replaying those episodes over time (McClelland et al. 1995; Kumaran et al. 2016). Replay during sleep was first observed in the hippocampus of rats (Wilson and McNaughton 1994), and it has since been measured in humans as well, during rest (Liu et al. 2019; Schuck and Niv 2019). Sleep seems to play an active role in moving memories from the fast system to the slow one (Klinzing et al. 2019). One reason for two systems is precisely to avoid what AI researchers call catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen 1989).
Plasticity. Connections change with use. And when we learn to read, a region of the visual cortex becomes specialised for written words, a process Dehaene and Cohen call neuronal recycling (Dehaene and Cohen 2007). New specialists are not only present from birth; they are formed during life.
Sparse and frugal. The human brain has about 86 billion neurons (Herculano-Houzel 2009) and runs on roughly 20 watts (Balasubramanian 2021). Energy budgets suggest that only a small share of cortical neurons can be strongly active at the same time, perhaps around one percent, although the exact figure is debated (Lennie 2003; Attwell and Laughlin 2001).



Figure 11. How the brain seems to be organised, and the part of the ecosystem each idea corresponds to. An analogy, my own, not a claim that the brain is built like software. Sources for each brain property are given in section 9.


Researchers who work on lifelong learning in machines draw the same lesson from biology: memory systems that learn at different speeds, replay, and modular, adaptable parts are among the mechanisms they consider most promising (Kudithipudi et al. 2022). If our best example of general intelligence is most likely a huge set of specialised, plastic sub-models, with a general coordinator, a fast memory and a slow learner, then I find it hard to believe that the best local AI will be one frozen, dense block.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
10. A memory outside the weights
Specialists need a memory they share. In Fast AI I argued that a large model should be used to build a structured memory, such as a knowledge graph experts can inspect and correct. In a local ecosystem, that memory becomes the common ground, and plays the role of the fast memory in section 9. Two kinds matter:

Knowledge: facts, rules, relations. “This customer always pays within 30 days.”
Episodes: what happened. “Last Tuesday this invoice was rejected because the supplier’s VAT number did not match.”

Keeping this memory outside the weights is what makes the system trustworthy. You can read it. You can correct a fact in one place, and every specialist benefits. You can delete something and know it is gone, which is very hard to guarantee once data has been used to train a model; removing its influence afterwards is an open research problem (Bourtoule et al. 2021). Retrieval also lets small models know far more than their weights hold (Borgeaud et al. 2022; Lewis et al. 2020).



Figure 12. Where knowledge lives matters. My own summary of the properties described in this section; on deletion, see (Bourtoule et al. 2021).


This is, for me, the strongest reason for running it locally. Privacy is not only protection. It is the condition for memory. People and companies will only let a system remember everything useful if they control where that memory lives.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
11. A way to keep learning
A memory lets a system look things up. It does not let it get better. Today’s models are trained once, frozen, and shipped. A local ecosystem can do better, because it sees the same kind of work every day, and because its specialists are small enough to update. I imagine a loop with two speeds, inspired by section 9:

Fast, during the day. The specialists work. Successes, corrections and failures are written to the memory as episodes. Nothing in the models changes.
Slow, at night. The system selects verified episodes, mixes them with examples of what the specialist already does well, updates the adapter, and tests the result against everything it was already good at. If it is better and has not forgotten anything, it is kept. If not, it is rolled back.

Each step has support in existing work. Mixing old examples with new ones, replay, is one of the most reliable ways to limit forgetting (Rolnick et al. 2019); brain-inspired versions of replay go further and replay internal representations instead of stored examples (Ven et al. 2020). Other methods protect the weights that matter most for old tasks (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017). Adapters forget less than full fine-tuning (Biderman et al. 2024). And using a machine’s idle time is starting to be studied as a resource in itself: sleep-time compute lets a model think about its context before questions arrive, reducing the work needed when they do (Lin et al. 2025). A broad review of continual learning describes the trade-offs between these approaches (Wang et al. 2024).
The test step deserves a little arithmetic, because it is where narrow specialists have a real advantage. If a specialist is right with probability p on a test set of n examples, the standard error of the measured accuracy is

\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.

With p = 0.9 and n = 2000, \sigma \approx 0.7 percentage points, so a drop of 2 points stands out at about three standard errors. Building 2000 good test cases for one narrow job is realistic. Building them for every ability of a general model is not.



Figure 13. Schematic, my own, not measured. A frozen model stays as good as the day it was shipped. A specialist that consolidates every night improves in small, tested steps. When an update makes it forget something, the test catches it and the update is rolled back.


The risks are real. A model trained repeatedly on its own outputs can degrade, a problem known as model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024). The risk is much lower when real data are kept and accumulated alongside generated data, instead of being replaced by it (Gerstgrasser et al. 2024). This is one more reason for a memory that keeps the real episodes, and for a loop that learns only from episodes verified by a test, a person or the real world, never from its own unchecked answers. And a model that changes every night is harder to certify. Small updates, strict tests, a memory that keeps the evidence, and the ability to roll back are not optional.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
12. Where the big models fit
None of this makes frontier models useless. It changes their role.
They become teachers: their knowledge can be passed to small models by distillation (Hinton et al. 2015), including their step-by-step explanations (Hsieh et al. 2023). The DeepSeek-R1 team, for example, released a family of small models, from 1.5 to 70 billion parameters, trained on the reasoning of its large model (DeepSeek-AI 2025). They become architects of memory: they read the documents and build the first version of the knowledge graph. And they become consultants: when the router meets something new, or a problem that needs broad reasoning across many domains, it can ask, with the user’s permission, and the verified answer becomes an episode the local system can learn from.

title: An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle
text:
14. Conclusion
I do not think we should wait for the big brain to come to us. The future I believe in is already within reach, and it is organised differently: specialists that are excellent at one thing, a router that knows who does what and when it does not know, a memory you own, a harness that is thin but keeps the essentials, and a careful loop that turns yesterday’s verified work into tomorrow’s skill.
The question will not only be “how much intelligence can I run locally?” It will be “how well is my local intelligence organised, what does it remember, and how does it learn?” Our own brain, most likely, already answers it that way.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text: Something different, just this once. This blog is usually about AI, machines and measurement. This essay is not. It is a personal detour into physics, written by someone who is neither a physicist nor a mathematician, following a question out of curiosity. Its follow-up, Decided in the Bulk, Written on the Boundary, brings the question back to AI.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
section: It must be simpler than this
text:
It must be simpler than this
I am not a physicist. I am not a mathematician. But one evening I opened a new physics paper, Holograms and Standard Models by Miyashita, Sekino and Susskind, and tried to follow it.
I got lost quickly. Fermions, ensembles, double-scaled limits, Feynman diagrams that look like flowers. And my first reaction was simple: something is wrong here. It must be easier. I believe the universe is fundamentally simple.
This essay is what happened when I followed that feeling. I didn’t find the answer. I found better questions, and maybe that is the point.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
The surface knows everything
The first surprise came from black holes. In the 1970s, Bekenstein and Hawking found that the information a black hole can hold depends on the area of its surface, not on its volume.

S = \frac{A}{4\,\ell_P^2}

In plain words: cover the horizon with tiny tiles, each the size of the smallest length physics knows, and you have counted everything inside. Double the size of the black hole and its information grows four times, not eight.



Figure 1. The surface knows everything. Left: a horizon covered with tiles, each the smallest area physics knows. Right: make a black hole twice as wide and the room inside grows eight times, but the information it can hold grows only four times, like its surface. Schematic, my own; the code is in figs.py.


This is strange. In everyday life a bigger box holds more things because it has more room inside. Here the inside seems to be written on the walls. Physicists call this the holographic principle: our three-dimensional world may be like an image projected from a flat surface.
So I asked myself: what if area and volume are not two different things? What if they are two faces of the same idea? It turns out physicists ask this too. Some say the area measures how much things are connected (entanglement) and the volume measures how complicated they are. Maybe space is just the shape that information takes when we look at it from inside.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
Everything from nothing
Einstein did not change physics with more complicated equations. He took one simple idea completely seriously: light moves at the same speed for everyone. So I wondered if we are looking in the wrong place. What if there is nothing at all, and that nothing is creating everything?
To my surprise, the paper I could not follow says something close to this. The authors put their model at infinite temperature. That sounds extreme, but it means something simple: every possibility is equally likely. No preference, no structure, no information. It is the state of maximum ignorance, the closest thing to “nothing” that quantum physics allows.
And from this featureless state they claim a whole small world appears: particles, forces, even the tiny energy of empty space. Their motto is “set it and forget it.” You choose one number, how big the system is, and the rest follows.
Others had similar dreams. Some physicists noticed that the energy of matter and the energy of gravity may cancel exactly, so a universe might cost nothing to make. John Wheeler said “it from bit”: reality built from yes-or-no answers, information before matter. Of course, their “nothing” still has laws of physics in it. Why there are laws at all is still a mystery.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
Grains within grains
Then another thought. What if we never reach the final piece? What if there is no end?
History points that way. We thought atoms were the bottom. Then we found the nucleus, then quarks. Each time the “fundamental” level turned out to be made of something else.
But the black hole formula seems to say no. If a region can hold only a limited amount of information, it cannot hide infinite layers inside. There must be a floor.
Unless the floor belongs only to us. What if what we call the universe is just one grain? The limit would apply inside our horizon, the part we can see, and not to everything. Some cosmologists already imagine this: space inflating forever, making bubble universes like ours, each one a grain, each with its own rules.
And it should work both ways. In 1987 physicists showed that a tiny bubble of very dense energy could grow into a new universe. From outside it would look like a small black hole that disappears. From inside it would be a whole cosmos, expanding, maybe one day full of people asking the same questions. A grain inside our grain. And maybe ours is a grain inside someone else’s.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
text:
The vertigo
At this point I felt something I did not expect. A kind of dizziness. Nothing creating everything. Grains inside grains. No final layer. Are we at the end of thinking, or just getting close to going a bit mad?
I don’t think it is madness. Pascal, more than three hundred years ago, wrote that the eternal silence of infinite spaces frightened him. Einstein said the most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible. The dizziness seems to be what you feel when you follow the questions honestly.
The hard part is not the physics. It is accepting that we may go from nothing to nothing, with no final answer waiting for us. We want an end. We tell stories with endings. We look for the cause behind the cause. Being told the chain may never close feels like losing the ground under your feet.

title: A Universe Without a Bottom
section: The meaning is in the middle
text:
The meaning is in the middle
Mathematics went through this once. In 1931 Kurt Gödel proved that mathematics can never be complete: there will always be true things it cannot prove. Many thought it was the end. It was not. Mathematics kept growing, and the open horizon became part of its beauty.
Maybe physics is the same. An end out of reach does not make the answers along the way less real. Feynman said he could live with doubt and not knowing, and that it was more interesting than having answers that might be wrong.
And “from nothing to nothing” forgets the middle. The middle is everything: stars, black holes, and someone on a quiet evening trying to understand a paper too difficult for them. If there is no final end, then asking is not a failure to arrive. Maybe it is what the universe does when it becomes complex enough to look at itself.
I started by believing the universe must be simple. I still believe it. But maybe simple does not mean finished.

The same question, turned into an experiment on an AI image generator.
