title: The Junior Colleague
text:
Analysis, October 2026. An analysis of Zhu et al., JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs (UIUC, Princeton, Google; arXiv 2610.21412, 15 October 2026), read in the light of my earlier essay Fast AI. Unless stated otherwise, numbers come from that paper. Figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py.
Abstract. Most of an AI agent’s calls to a large language model end in a multiple-choice pick: which tool, which argument, stop or continue. Zhu and colleagues ask whether these picks can be handed to a small decision model that answers in milliseconds, without losing task success. Their answer is yes, under three conditions: the decision model is tested inside the agent rather than on isolated questions, it is used only when its confidence clears a threshold fitted on the agent’s own runs, and it is trained on the states the agent actually reaches, including after its own mistakes. Under these conditions, an open 4B model made customer-service agents 86.3% cheaper and 2.5 times faster with no detectable loss of success. The gains were small in coding agents, and the method failed badly on a rule the model had never seen, until thresholds were refitted. I argue that this is the missing piece of Fast AI: a fast path at the level of single choices, which knows when it is unsure and learns its habits from the slow path.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
1. The question
In Fast AI I argued that automation should learn slowly, once, and act fast every time, keeping the large model for the exceptions. The essay left one practical question open: inside a running agent, how do you know which steps are routine, and what answers them if not the large model?
The JevAgentHarness paper addresses exactly this. Its starting observation is simple. Watch an agent work and count what it decides. A customer asks to cancel an order; the agent must choose to look up the order, cancel it, or ask the customer first; then which order; then which reason from a fixed list; then whether the task is done. Each of these is a call to a large language model that reads the whole context and writes its answer token by token, in seconds. Yet almost every one ends in picking one item from a list the harness already knows.
The authors identify eight such decision points in one step of an agent loop: three that choose what the agent does (the tool, its arguments, or the next action) and five that control the loop (write memory, read memory, reflect after a failure, stop, or route the step to a cheaper model). Their research question is how a harness can delegate these choices “to a fast, cheap decision model when the model is reliable, so that agentic tasks become faster and cheaper with little loss of success.”



Figure 1. Schematic. Today the large model makes every choice of the loop. With a decision model, the routine choices are answered in milliseconds, and the large model is called only where the decision model is unsure.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
2. Background: decision models
Decision models are a new class of model built for this kind of choice. Given a context and a question with fixed options, they return a probability for each option instead of generating text. The best known is Jev, released by TypeSafe in September 2026 and presented as a “System One” model, after Daniel Kahneman’s fast, intuitive mode of thinking (TypeSafe announcement). Its weights and size are not public. In one episode recorded by Zhu and colleagues, a call to Jev took 28% of an LLM call’s time and 2.6% of its price; the project repository estimates about 0.15 s and $0.0001 for a typical coding-agent state.
Open counterparts appeared within weeks, among them Intern-Decision, StartLux-Decision and OpenJev. So did the first independent evaluations, which are worth reading before trusting any of these models. As a cheap judge, Jev detected alignment failures such as sycophancy and prompt injection about as well as a reference LLM scorer, at a fraction of the cost (Guo et al., 2026). As a rubric judge, it was found “cheaper, faster, and wrong in the same places” as LLMs (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026). Adversarial tests show that small edits to a question can flip its typed answers (JevAdvBench), and one study reports that swapping the order of “yes” and “no” changes many of its answers (arXiv 2610.00346).
The idea itself is older than these models. A classifier that may abstain when unsure is known as selective classification (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017); one that hands cases to an expert is learning to defer (Mozannar and Sontag, 2020). Routers and cascades such as FrugalGPT and RouteLLM apply it to whole requests, and agents that think “fast and slow”, such as SwiftSage or the Talker-Reasoner architecture, apply it to whole steps. What is new in JevAgentHarness is the grain: one typed choice at a time, inside the agent, with a threshold per kind of choice.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
3. The approach
The paper has three parts, one for each condition the authors believe a decision model needs to be useful.
A benchmark at three levels. AgentDecisionBench tests decision models on isolated questions (level 1), at each step of recorded agent runs, where answers are scored but not executed (level 2), and in control of a running agent, where every choice changes what comes next (level 3). Because public benchmarks only check the end of a run, the authors built DecisionGym, a simulated customer-service desk in the style of τ-bench, which knows the acceptable next steps at every reachable state, including after detours. Each task offers 68 tools in shuffled order, among them 31 near-duplicates of the core tools.
A harness that asks, then decides whether to trust. JevAgentHarness plugs into existing harnesses such as mini-SWE-agent or the pi terminal agent through their hooks. At each routine choice, it asks the decision model a typed multiple-choice question: tools, fixed-list or yes/no argument values, or spans to copy from the context. In the main mode, the cascade, the answer is used only when the decision model’s confidence c clears a threshold. Otherwise the large model decides as usual. The paper derives the threshold from a simple cost argument: delegating is worth it when

c \;\ge\; q_L - \frac{\Delta C}{V},

where q_L is how often the large model gets this choice right, \Delta C the price of the saved call and V the cost of a wrong choice. The small model may be slightly less accurate than the large one, as long as the saving covers the extra risk. In practice, the agent first runs on separate tasks while the decision model answers silently (shadow mode), and the threshold is fitted on these runs for each decision point. With Jev and Gemini 3.5 Flash, the fitted thresholds were 1.00 for tools and 0.99 for arguments: only near-certain answers are used.



Figure 2. The threshold rule of Zhu and colleagues, with illustrative values of my own. When a call costs little against what a wrong choice costs, the threshold sits just under the large model’s own accuracy.


A model trained on the agent’s own states. AgentDecision-4B is Qwen3-4B with a LoRA adapter. The harness ran 587 training tasks and recorded every decision state, 15,694 in all. To include states after errors, a scripted policy repeated mistakes seen during development, an idea from imitation learning (Ross et al., 2011), so that 30.9% of the states follow a mistake. Jev’s probabilities served as soft labels, mixed with the correct answer, under a loss that also keeps the probabilities calibrated. A second stage of reinforcement learning inside the agent loop rewarded success with fewer LLM calls.
The protocol is careful: the models, tasks and tests were registered before the main runs, each delegation was tested alone for non-inferiority (less than 3 points of success lost, at the 5% level, with a correction for multiple tests), and only then were the passing delegations combined and tested on new tasks.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
4. Findings

4.1 Isolated scores misrank decision models
On isolated questions, the models were within about 5 points of each other. Inside a running agent, their task success spread over 57 points. StartLux-9B, the most accurate on isolated tool choice at 92.2%, solved 69.5% of tasks. AgentDecision-4B, at 89.3%, solved 91.5%. The difference lies in the hard states, such as the moments when the right move is to ask the customer before an irreversible action: there, AgentDecision-4B answered 67.4% correctly and Jev 58.3%. Accuracy on recorded agent steps ranked the models nearly as task success did (Kendall correlation 0.84).



Figure 3. Accuracy on isolated questions against tasks solved when the model makes the agent’s tool choices, on shifted customer-service tasks. Data from Zhu et al., Figure 4b.




4.2 A fitted threshold protects success
With a fitted threshold, Jev made 27.2% of the tool choices and 20.8% of the argument choices, cutting cost by 14.2% without changing the outcome of any of 500 tasks. Without a threshold, letting Jev make every tool choice lost 19.0 points of success; a fixed threshold of 0.5 lost 21.5. The threshold, not the model, is what makes delegation safe.


4.3 Training on the agent’s own states works
Supervised training on the agent’s own states raised the 4B model from 13.5% to 96.0% of shifted tasks solved, for 2.2 GPU-hours. The same recipe raised StartLux-4B from 49.0% to 98.0%. The reinforcement-learning stage added no measurable gain, which the authors report plainly. The student beat its teacher: Jev solved 82.0% of the same tasks. On one L4 graphics card, AgentDecision-4B answered in a median of 31 ms, against 809 ms for a call to Gemini 3.5 Flash.



Figure 4. Tasks solved on shifted customer-service tasks, with different decision models making the agent’s tool choices. Data from Zhu et al., Table 3.




4.4 The gains depend on how much the choices repeat



Figure 5. LLM cost saved, with the change in task success against the large model alone, in four settings. Data from Zhu et al., Tables 1 and 2.



Customer service. On 500 new tasks, AgentDecision-4B on its own graphics card made 99.9% of the tool choices and 75.0% of the argument choices, saving 4.5 LLM calls per task: 86.3% cheaper, 2.5 times faster, success within half a point of the large model alone.
Text games. On ALFWorld, a 4B model trained on the game’s states made the agent 89.0% cheaper and about twice as fast, with higher success, and kept these gains in unseen rooms.
Coding agents. Actions are free text, so the decision model could only choose which LLM writes each step. Savings were 7.0–10.5%, and success varied by harness.



4.5 Fast models fail confidently on new rules
On harder tasks with a cancellation rule no model was trained on, AgentDecision-4B made most cancel-or-ship choices but got only 81.6% of them right, and the agent solved 3.0% of the tasks, against 88.0% for the large model alone. Refitting the threshold restored success; retraining on the rule raised the model’s accuracy from 76.5% to 95.3%. In the same vein, all 34 of Jev’s failed tasks began with an irreversible wrong tool choice, usually cancelling where the agent should have asked.

title: The Junior Colleague
section: 5. Analysis: what this means for Fast AI
text:
5. Analysis: what this means for Fast AI
Fast AI proposed a split: deep networks perceive, a knowledge graph remembers, trees decide, and the agentic loop is kept for the exceptions. The paper does not test this architecture, but its results bear on it in five ways.
Decision models fill the gap between trees and the large model. Gradient-boosted trees remain my choice when a decision rests on structured features. But many choices in a process come as text: a customer message, a chat history, a ticket. These used to fall to the large model by default. A small decision model now handles them in milliseconds, with a probability attached.
“Knowing when unsure” becomes an engineering step. Fast AI required every fast model to know when to hand over, without saying how. The paper’s answer is concrete: run in shadow mode, measure, fit one threshold per kind of choice, refit when something changes. Finding 4.2 shows this step matters more than the choice of model.
The habit loop is the training loop. Finding 4.3 is the habit-forming step of Fast AI, made measurable. The slow, expensive teachers, Jev and the large model, label the agent’s own experience once. The fast student learns the habits of this agent in this domain, including how to recover from its own errors. Logged deferrals become the next round of training data.



Figure 6. Fast AI with a decision model. Each listed choice goes to a small decision model. Above its threshold, it decides; below, the large model, an agent or a person does. The logs, including the agent’s mistakes, are used to retrain the model and refit the thresholds, which are tested in shadow mode before they are trusted.


The knowledge graph still matters, perhaps more. A decision model is only as good as its options, and Finding 4.5 shows what happens when the rules change under it. In a well-built system, the graph supplies the options (which tools apply to this supplier, which approvers are valid for this amount) and holds the rules in a form a person can read and correct. When a rule changes, the change is made once in the graph, and the thresholds are refitted. Habits in weights are fast; habits in a graph are auditable. A serious system needs both.
It fits the local ecosystem. A 4B model on one graphics card is the kind of small specialist I described in An Ecosystem, Not an Oracle. NVIDIA researchers make the same argument for agents in general: most of what agents do is narrow and repetitive, and small models can do it more economically (Belcak et al., 2025). Decision models push this furthest, because picking an option is far narrower than writing.

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
6. Limits and open questions
The paper is careful about its limits, and they shape how far its results can be carried.

External validity. All tasks are in English, most runs use Gemini models, and the most striking numbers come from the authors’ own environment, DecisionGym. Independent replication on real workloads is the next step.
Fitted to one agent. Thresholds and trained models are fitted to one agent’s runs. A new agent, new tools or a new task family call for refitting and, for the best accuracy, retraining.
Silent drift. Finding 4.5 shows that confidence does not drop on its own when rules change. The authors suggest tracking the share of answers above the threshold; I would add the shape-based monitoring of What a Quiet Screen Cannot See.
Irreversible actions. A confident wrong choice at an irreversible step ends the task. The authors warn that a decision-model guard should never be the only control on such an action, and that adapters should not be used as security boundaries.
Statistics. The main tests show that success drops by less than 3 points; showing equal success would need an equivalence test. The authors did not compare against learned routers such as RouteLLM on the same tasks.
Licence. The trained weights are released under a non-commercial licence, partly because they are trained on outputs of a proprietary model.

Two questions seem open to me. First, how much of the gain survives when the options themselves must be discovered, rather than listed by the harness? Second, can the threshold and the knowledge graph be kept in step automatically, so that a rule change in the graph triggers refitting before it triggers failures?

title: The Junior Colleague
text:
7. Conclusion
The large model was never meant to answer “which of these three tools?” ten thousand times a day. It was meant to handle what is new, and to teach.
JevAgentHarness shows a careful way to arrange this: ask a small decision model first, trust it only above a threshold fitted on your own runs, test it on your own work rather than on a leaderboard, and train it on the states your agent really reaches, mistakes included. When the choices repeat, the result is an agent several times faster and far cheaper, with no detectable loss of success. When the world changes, the same discipline of shadow mode, refitting and retraining is what keeps it safe.
That is a junior colleague in the best sense: fast on the routine, honest about what they do not know, and getting better every month from what the seniors decide. It is also Fast AI, one choice at a time.

Read next · Fast AI Why the large model should build the memory once, instead of reasoning through every run.


The views in this analysis are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
A provocative paper, on purpose. This is a position paper, written to argue one side as strongly as I can, in the form of a short scientific paper. It states a thesis, defines its terms, gives arguments and evidence, and ends with predictions that could prove it wrong. It is not a neutral survey. A follow-up to The Interface Is Data. Figures are my own, drawn with the code in figs.py.
Abstract. Each generation of programming has turned what people used to write into something the machine generates: machine code into the output of assemblers, assembly into the output of compilers, boilerplate into the output of frameworks. I argue that agentic coding, in which a language model plans, edits, runs and repairs code inside a loop, is the next step on this ladder, and a larger one than it looks. The thesis is that the agentic loop is both the next IDE and the next programming language. I define a program as a tuple P = (I, T, K, \Gamma) of intent, executable checks, context and tools, and the agent as a stochastic compiler that is correct only up to the checks. From this definition follow four arguments (historical, structural, economic, empirical), one central consequence (the precision of the new language is the strength of its checks), and four predictions that can be measured within a few years. I end with the strongest objections, including Dijkstra’s, and the evidence that currently cuts against me.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
1. Introduction
Programming languages are usually described by their syntax and semantics. A more useful description, for the argument here, is what a person has to write and what the machine produces from it. By that measure, the history of programming is a ladder. On each rung, people stopped writing one thing and started writing something more abstract, while the old thing kept existing as output.



Figure 1. Schematic. Each generation of programming turned what people used to write into what the step above generates. The examples are illustrative.


Since code-generating language models appeared (Chen et al. 2021), the obvious question has been whether they are a better autocomplete or something else. Andrej Karpathy framed neural networks as “Software 2.0” (Karpathy 2017) and, more recently, described prompting models in English as a new kind of programming (Karpathy 2025). I take a narrower and more testable position. I do not claim that English replaces programming languages. I claim that the unit a person writes is changing from code to a bundle of intent and checks, and that the environment a person works in is changing from an editor to a loop. If both hold, then the agentic loop is, in the plain historical sense, the next language and the next IDE.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
2. Background
The ladder. When FORTRAN appeared in 1957, its designers faced deep scepticism that machine-generated code could approach hand-written assembly; much of their effort went into the optimiser, precisely to win that argument (Backus 1978). They won, and the pattern repeated with every later level of abstraction.
Natural language as code. The idea of programming in English is old. Jean Sammet discussed it in 1966 (Sammet 1966); Edsger Dijkstra called it foolish in the late 1970s, arguing that the precision of formal notation is a feature, not a burden (Dijkstra, n.d.). Program synthesis research pursued the goal from specifications and examples for decades (Gulwani et al. 2017), with success in narrow domains.
Agents that code. Language models trained on code reached usable accuracy on small functions in 2021 (Chen et al. 2021). Since then, agents that read a repository, edit files, run tests and iterate have been evaluated on real GitHub issues (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024). The productivity evidence is mixed: a controlled experiment found developers 55.8% faster on a small, well-specified task with an AI pair programmer (Peng et al. 2023), while a randomised study of experienced open-source developers on their own mature repositories found them 19% slower with early-2025 tools (Becker et al. 2025).

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
3. A minimal definition
I define a program, in the agentic sense, as a tuple

P = (I,\; T,\; K,\; \Gamma),

where I is the intent, what is wanted, stated in words and examples; T is a set of executable checks (tests, types, properties, linters) that a candidate implementation must pass; K is the context, the repository and its conventions; and \Gamma is the set of tools and interfaces the agent may use, described as data in the sense of The Interface Is Data.
An agent A maps a program to code, c = A(P). A classical compiler is deterministic and preserves meaning by construction. An agent does neither. It is a stochastic compiler: its output can vary between runs, and it is correct only in the weak sense that

T(c) = \text{pass}.

Call the specification gap of P the set of behaviours that pass T but are not what I meant. The whole discipline of the new language is to make this gap small: by sharpening I, by strengthening T, and by having a person review what remains.



Figure 2. Schematic. The agent as a stochastic compiler. The program is the tuple of intent, checks, context and tools. The agent produces code, which is checked automatically and then reviewed by a person. Failed checks send the agent back; review refines the intent and strengthens the checks.


Under this definition, the concepts of the familiar toolchain map onto new ones.

Table 1. The toolchain, translated. My own mapping.


Today
In the agentic loop




Source file
Intent, examples and checks: (I, T)


Compiler
Agent: c = A(P), stochastic


Type checker
Tests, types and properties: T(c)


Standard library
Tools and interfaces: \Gamma


Build configuration
Repository context and conventions: K


Debugger
Decision log and execution trace of the agent


Code review
Review of intent first, then of the diff


Editor
Plan, diff and checks panes; typing as fallback

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
4. Four arguments
4.1 Historical. Every previous rung of the ladder was resisted on the grounds that generated output was slower, less precise or less trustworthy than what experts wrote by hand (Backus 1978). Each time, the generated output improved, the cost of writing by hand stayed the same, and the line crossed. Nothing in the current situation suggests the pattern has stopped; the objections raised today are the same three.
4.2 Structural. Brooks distinguished the essential complexity of software, deciding precisely what it must do, from its accidental complexity, the effort of expressing that decision in a particular language and toolset (Brooks 1987). Under the definition above, a person writes I and T, which carry the essential complexity, and the agent handles the expression, which is accidental. This is the division of labour every abstraction has aimed for, achieved at a higher level than before. Tests, long promoted as a design discipline (Beck 2002), become the main way to state that essential part.
4.3 Economic. The cost of producing a correct change has three parts: writing it, checking it, and understanding it later. Agentic coding drives the first towards zero and leaves the other two. A rational team will therefore spend its people where the cost remains, on intent, checks and review, which is exactly the shift from editor to loop that the thesis predicts. The IDE follows the work: when typing is no longer the bottleneck, an environment organised around typing is the wrong shape.
4.4 Empirical. Agents now resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation (Jimenez et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024), a task that requires reading context, editing several files and passing existing tests: the full loop of Figure 2, not autocomplete. The negative result of Becker et al. (2025) is important and I return to it in §6, but it measures an early tool generation, on large mature repositories, with developers who had little experience of the new way of working. That is close to measuring FORTRAN in 1957 with assembly experts.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
5. Predictions
A position paper should be falsifiable. If the thesis is right, the following should be observed in professional software over the next few years; if they are not, it is wrong.

H1. Authorship shifts. The share of merged changes whose code was primarily produced by an agent keeps rising in professional repositories, measurable from commit metadata and tool logs.
H2. Checks grow relative to code. In human-written lines, the ratio of tests, types and specifications to implementation rises.
H3. Review becomes the main human cost. Time spent reviewing and specifying exceeds time spent writing code, in the same teams that adopt agents.
H4. Gains follow the strength of checks. Productivity gains from agents are larger where T is strong (well-tested code with clear conventions) than where it is weak, other things equal. This is the most direct test of claim 3.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
6. Objections
Natural language is too imprecise (Dijkstra). This is right, and it is the most important objection. But the program in §3 is not prose alone. Its precision lives in T, in K and in review, as it always has in teams where a person states a need and an engineer implements it. The objection becomes a design rule: wherever precision matters, state it as a check, not as a sentence.
A stochastic compiler cannot be trusted. Deterministic compilers can be trusted because their meaning-preservation can be argued once. A stochastic compiler cannot; it must be checked every time. This raises the value of T and of review, and it means that for code where checks are weak and errors are costly, the old way should remain. The thesis predicts a shift in the default, not the end of hand-written code.
Developers are slower, not faster (Becker et al. 2025). If replications on strong-check repositories, with experienced users of current tools, continue to find slowdowns, H4 fails and so does much of this paper. I consider this the most likely way for me to be wrong.
Code is still the artefact that runs. Yes, as assembly still runs. The thesis does not say code disappears; it says it stops being the thing people mainly write. Like assembly, it remains the layer that can always be read, and to which the machine is held.
Literate programming tried this. Knuth argued that programs should be written for people first (Knuth 1984). Literate programming kept the person as the author of the code. The difference here is that the person is the author of the intent and the checks, and the code is derived.

title: Intent Is the Source
text:
7. Conclusion
Every generation of programmers was told that the next level of abstraction was a toy, and each time the toy became the language. I have argued, on purpose without hedging, that the agentic loop is the next such level: the source becomes intent plus checks, the compiler becomes a stochastic agent held to those checks, and the IDE becomes a place to steer and review. The definition makes one consequence precise. The new language is exactly as rigorous as its checks, so the craft of programming does not disappear; it moves into specification, testing and judgement. Four predictions make the claim testable. I expect to be partly wrong. I would rather be wrong in a way that can be measured.

Read next · The Interface Is Data How MCP and the agentic loop change what we call an API.


The views in this paper are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
A provocative paper, on purpose. A position paper in the form of a short scientific paper: a thesis, a model, a simulation, and predictions that could prove it wrong. It follows Review the Intent, Not the Diff, which kept review and changed its object; this paper asks whether we need the review at all. Figures are my own, drawn and simulated with the code in figs.py.
Abstract. Human approval of every pull request became standard when code was written by hand and defects found late were expensive. I model the review gate as an investment that pays when p \cdot d \cdot \Delta C > r: the chance a change still carries a defect after automated checks, times the share a reviewer catches, times the late-fix cost avoided, must exceed the cost of the gate. Agentic coding shrinks the late-fix cost of most changes, but not where harm survives a revert. The model therefore yields a rule rather than a ban: approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else. Watching means rules in every session and a daily audit of the whole codebase. The approval that remains is a thin gate placed late, at the point of no return, rather than at the merge. In a simulation of a team merging 40 changes a day, the audit and the thin gate together leave a third of today’s latent defects and the same number of irreversible incidents, for about 80 minutes of people time a day instead of 16 hours. I state the conditions under which this holds and five predictions to test it.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
1. Introduction
For most changes, nobody should have to approve the pull request. The usual answer is that this would end in chaos. I do not think so, and the reason is economic. Review is a control, and every control has a price. We paid it because the gate was the cheapest place to catch a defect: minutes at review against days once it reached users.
Agentic coding changes the price on both sides. Rules can be enforced inside every session instead of at its end. A fix takes an agent minutes, and a flag can switch a change off in seconds. Correction is cheap now, and I believe that is what changes the whole picture. Human attention stays expensive, and the gate spends it on every change, whether or not that change needs it.
Correction is not cheap everywhere. Deleted data, leaked credentials or money sent to the wrong account cannot be taken back by a revert. Hence the rule: approve what you cannot undo; watch everything else. Where approval remains, it must come late and stay small, or it brings little.



Figure 1. Today, every change waits for a person. In the proposal, everything merges when the checks pass. Only an action that cannot be undone waits, late, at a thin gate where a person decides; everything else is released. Every night, an audit of the whole codebase tells the team what to fix and which rules to tighten.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
2. Background: what review was for
Inspections. Formal code inspection began at IBM in the 1970s as a defect-removal step (Fagan 1976), justified by the claim that a defect costs one to two orders of magnitude more to fix in operation than in development (Boehm 1981). The empirical basis of that curve is thinner than its fame (Bossavit 2015), and agile practice argued that integration and automated tests flatten it (Beck 1999).
What modern review finds. Lightweight review replaced inspections in most teams (Rigby and Bird 2013). At Microsoft, developers named finding defects as their first motivation, yet most comments concerned code improvement and understanding (Bacchelli and Bird 2013); a later study was titled Code Reviews Do Not Find Bugs (Czerwonka et al. 2015). About three quarters of the issues found concern evolvability rather than behaviour (Mäntylä and Lassenius 2009; Beller et al. 2014). At Google, people valued education, norms, gatekeeping and accident prevention most (Sadowski, Söderberg, et al. 2018).
Evidence for review. Components with low review coverage had more post-release defects in three open-source projects (McIntosh et al. 2014), and careful reading improves quality (Kemerer and Paulk 2009). On approval, the largest survey of delivery performance found that external approval slowed delivery without reducing failed changes, and recommended lightweight peer review instead (Forsgren et al. 2018).
Agentic review today. The Claude Code team at Anthropic already lets low-risk changes merge without a person when automated review passes, and reports more merged changes and fewer reverts (Claude Code team, Anthropic 2026). The rule proposed here replaces their risk score with a simpler question and makes no-approval the default.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
section: 3. A cost model of the gate
text:
3. A cost model of the gate
Consider one change. Let p be the probability that it still carries a defect after all automated checks; d the share of such defects a human reviewer catches; \Delta C = C_{\text{late}} - C_{\text{review}} the cost avoided by catching it at review; and r the full cost of the gate for one change, including reading, waiting and context switches. The gate pays for itself when

p \, d \, \Delta C > r .
\tag{1}
The late cost is the work of the fix plus the harm done while the defect lives. If harm accrues at a rate k and the defect is found after a time \tau,

C_{\text{late}} \approx c_{\text{fix}} + k \, \tau .
\tag{2}
What agents change. Session rules can lower p: an agent can be made to add tests for every changed behaviour, keep coverage of changed lines above a threshold and follow a conventions file, and checks delivered while code is written are the ones developers act on (Sadowski, Aftandilian, et al. 2018). This is not automatic, since code written with AI assistants can be less secure (Pearce et al. 2022; Perry et al. 2023), so the simulation keeps p the same under every policy. Meanwhile r does not fall: careful review proceeds at a few hundred lines an hour (Kemerer and Paulk 2009), volume rises, and waiting grows roughly as \rho/(1-\rho) with reviewer utilisation \rho (Kingman 1961).
The main assumption. The term that moves most is \Delta C. Assumption A: for most defects, an agent can produce a correct fix within an hour of the report, and a flag or a rollback can stop the harm within minutes. Under A, c_{\text{fix}} is small, flags cap k (Humble and Farley 2010), and an audit caps \tau. Agents resolve a meaningful share of real repository issues under controlled evaluation (Jimenez et al. 2024), and the best teams in Forsgren et al. (2018) already restored service in under an hour; neither measures agent-made fixes in production, so prediction H3 tests A directly.



Figure 2. Schematic. Before agents, a defect cost far more to fix the later it was found, a curve whose exact shape is disputed (Bossavit 2015). With agents, under Assumption A, a late fix costs little more than an early one. Harm that cannot be undone stays expensive.


Where the rule comes from. Assumption A flattens the cost curve only for harm that a revert removes. When harm persists after a revert, k\tau stays large however quickly the defect is found, and the gate still pays (the red point in Figure 3). Everything else drifts below the break-even line. The model does not say “never review”; it says exactly where review still pays.



Figure 3. The break-even condition of Equation 1, for d = 0.5. Review pays only when defects are likely and late fixes are costly. Agents move ordinary changes into the green region; changes that cannot be undone stay in the amber one. Positions are illustrative, not measured.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
4. The rule in practice
What cannot be undone. A change is a one-way door (Bezos 2016) when its harm survives a revert: data destroyed or exposed, money moved, credentials or signing keys changed, a public interface released outside the team, a message sent to customers. The list is explicit, versioned and part of the session contract. Code that touches it merges like any other; its irreversible step waits at the thin gate (§5). Sessions steered from outside the team belong to the same category: an outsider’s issue or a web page can direct an agent (Greshake et al. 2023), and a planted backdoor or a leaked secret cannot be undone either. The contract records where each session’s instructions came from, so such sessions are flagged automatically.
What watching means. Every change merges on green, and everything that is not a one-way door is released without waiting. It is watched at three points (Table 1): before the merge by a session contract enforced by the agent and CI; after it by flags and monitoring; and once a day by an audit that reads the whole codebase and production signals and writes a short report that the team reads instead of forty diffs. When a problem keeps reappearing, the team turns it into a rule, so the contract gradually absorbs what reviewers used to write in comments.
What the audit sees that a pre-merge check cannot. Fast checks belong in the contract. The audit adds slow checks such as mutation testing and fuzzing, patterns across changes, production signals since yesterday’s merges, and trends people can judge before any rule encodes them. A per-change reviewer misses the second and third kind too.

Table 1. A minimal session contract and audit. Thresholds and exact checks are for each team to set; the split is the point. What can be decided per change is enforced by machines; what needs judgement is batched once a day for people.

Coverage

Integrity

Conventions

The integrity rule stops the most common failure of coding agents, an agent that edits a test until it passes. Coverage is paired with mutation testing because coverage alone is a weak measure of test quality (Inozemtseva and Holmes 2014) and becomes a target once enforced (Strathern 1997); mutation testing measures whether tests notice a change in behaviour (Papadakis et al. 2019).
Who is accountable. The person who starts a session owns what it merges. Steering the agent and looking at its output is part of writing, and it stays. What disappears is the second person whose approval was required.
Intent changes. The previous essay sent every change of intent to a person before merging. The rule refines that: a change to a contract or invariant that can be reverted merges, but never silently. It updates its decision record, and the team reads it the next morning. Only intent that guards a one-way door meets the thin gate.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
5. The thin gate
Where the remaining gate sits and how much it asks decide whether it is worth having. A gate placed early and made thick, with a person reading every diff of every risky change, brings little. A gate placed late and kept thin keeps most of the value that is left.
Late: at the point of no return, not at the merge. Merging is reversible; code that touches a one-way door is safe until it runs. The irreversible act comes later: running the migration, rotating the key, sending the message, turning on the flag that moves money. The gate belongs there. The person judges what will actually run, with real data and configuration; the approval cannot go stale; and the gate holds back one action, not the team.
Thin: a few questions with evidence, not a diff. Reading code is slow, and reviews get shallower as changes grow (Kemerer and Paulk 2009). At the point of no return, five questions suffice (Figure 4). What exactly cannot be undone? What did a rehearsal, such as a dry run on a copy of production, show? What is affected, and can the action be staged? What is the way back, and has it been tested? Who asked, and did any instruction come from outside the team? The agent prepares the answers; the person checks them and chooses to go, to stage the action, or to stop. Staged releases are standard practice when an effect is uncertain (Beyer et al. 2016).



Figure 4. Schematic of a thin gate, with an illustrative example. The person answers five questions from evidence the agent prepared, instead of reading a diff. The gate is late, thin and rare.


In the terms of Equation 1, a thin, late gate raises d, because the person examines evidence about the one thing that matters, lowers r, because the decision takes minutes and is rarely needed, and sits where \Delta C is largest. A thick, early gate does the opposite on all three counts. One case needs more than five questions: a session steered from outside the team, where the danger hides in the code itself. There a person reads the diff or, better, the work is redone in a session the team steers.
Rare: keep it thin on purpose. Gates grow. Every incident adds an item to the list, and a long enough list turns the thin gate back into the old one, approved by tired people who no longer read. Track its load: the share of changes that reach it and the minutes per decision. When the same kind of action keeps arriving, make it undoable instead of adding approvers: soft deletes, schema changes that expand before they contract (Ambler and Sadalage 2006), keys that can be rolled back, releases region by region. Each piece of reversibility moves a class of changes from “approve” to “watch”. The best gate is one with less and less to do.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
6. A simulation
I simulated a team under five policies: a gate on every change (today’s common practice), no gate and no audit, an audit alone, the audit with the thin gate (the proposal), and a gate on every change with the audit. Each change may carry a reversible defect; one in twenty also carries an irreversible step, which may itself be defective. A defective irreversible step that runs unstopped is an irreversible incident: the nightly audit comes too late for it. The parameters (Table 2) are chosen rather than measured and, where I had to choose, generous to review.

Table 2. Simulation parameters. The audit includes production signals, so monitoring counts as part of the watch, not as users. The review queue is optimistic for the gate: reviewers start as soon as they are free. A value of d = 0.5 is high for functional defects given what review is known to find (Mäntylä and Lassenius 2009; Czerwonka et al. 2015).

Right: irreversible incidents per month, with the people time each policy costs per day. The audit does most of the work on reversible defects; the thin gate does the work on irreversible ones.

Chaos is real, but it is not the proposal. With no gate and no audit, latent defects double and irreversible incidents double. The critics are right about that policy, not about the alternative.
Each mechanism does one job. The audit alone cuts latent defects to a third of today’s, but leaves irreversible incidents at the chaos level, because a nightly audit finds them after the harm. The thin gate alone brings incidents back to today’s level, for 20 minutes a day. Together they beat today’s practice on reversible defects and match it on irreversible ones, at a twelfth of the people time. If the evidence at the thin gate lets it stop 80% of defective steps instead of 50%, incidents fall to 0.4 a month, well below today’s.
The price of the full gate. Adding a gate on every change to the audit lowers latent defects from 3.3 to 1.6 and does not reduce irreversible incidents, for 16 hours a day: about 10 engineer-hours for every day of latent defects it prevents (16 h ÷ 1.7 ≈ 9.4). Does a latent defect in this part of the system cost more than 10 engineer-hours a day? For a reversible defect in an internal tool, rarely. For a payment flow, easily, and that is a one-way door with its own thin gate.
Speed and reach of the watch. By Little’s law (Little 1961), latent defects equal the rate at which they enter times how long they stay. A gate removes at most the factor (1-d), here a half; an audit shortens the stay, here by a factor of six. But the audit may see only a share c of defects, the rest being found by users. The proposal then beats today’s practice when

c > d \left(1 + \frac{h_{\text{users}}}{h_{\text{audit}}}\right).
\tag{3}
In plain words, the watch must see more kinds of defect than a reviewer would have caught, and the slower it is, the more it must see. With the values of Table 2, an audit that finds what it sees in about two days must see at least 60% of defects, and one that takes five days, 75% (Figure 6). If a team’s defects are mostly of a kind no machine can notice, the rule fails for that team, and Equation 3 says so before any harm is done. Measure c first, and where it falls below the bound, keep reviewing changes to that part of the code until the watch improves.



Figure 6. How much must the audit see? Defects waiting to be found without a gate but with an audit, compared with today’s gate, against the share of defects the audit can see, for d = 0.5. Below the black line, the proposal does better than today; circles mark the thresholds. Lines follow Equation 3; the simulation agrees within 0.04.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
7. Predictions and a test protocol
Speed is not a useful test: removing a gate obviously speeds up merging. The thesis stands or falls on quality and on its assumptions. For teams that adopt the rule, compared with similar teams that keep the gate:

H1. No loss of stability. Change failure rate and time to restore service (Forsgren et al. 2018) are no worse, within a margin fixed in advance, and irreversible incidents do not rise.
H2. The watch sees far enough. The share of defects found first by the audit or monitoring rather than by users, an estimate of c, exceeds the bound of Equation 3, and defects are found sooner.
H3. Fixes are cheap (Assumption A). For defects found by the audit, the median time from report to merged fix is under one working hour, and a flag or rollback contains the harm before the fix lands.
H4. The report is used. At least half of the audit’s findings are fixed or explicitly dismissed within a week. An audit nobody reads turns the proposal into the chaos case.
H5. The gate stays thin. The share of changes reaching the thin gate and the minutes per decision stay small, and fall as more actions are made undoable.

Protocol. In a stepped-wedge design, teams adopt the rule one at a time, in random order, over several months, so every team is observed under both policies and calendar effects are controlled. H1 is a pre-registered non-inferiority test; H2 to H5 and lead time are secondary outcomes, measured from repository, pipeline and incident logs rather than self-reports, since teams cannot be blinded. If H1, H2 or H3 fails, the thesis is wrong for the teams studied.

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
8. Objections and limitations
“Review demonstrably reduces defects” (McIntosh et al. 2014). Compared with no review, on hand-written code, yes. The relevant comparison is review against watching, which H1 and H2 test. The recommendation of peer review in Forsgren et al. (2018) rests on data that predate agents; extending it is an extrapolation.
“Review is how teams share knowledge” (Bacchelli and Bird 2013; Sadowski, Söderberg, et al. 2018). It was. The replacement is deliberate: decision records, conventions, and a daily report read by the whole team rather than forty diffs each read by one person.
People adapt. Without a reviewer, authors may grow careless, or more careful because they alone own the result. The simulation holds p fixed; H1 measures the net effect.
Compliance. Some standards require custom code to be reviewed before release; PCI DSS sets conditions on who may review when the review is manual (PCI Security Standards Council 2022). Whether automated review satisfies them is for auditors to decide; where it does not, the code joins the list of one-way doors.
Loss of skill. Automation leaves people responsible for rare, hard cases while removing the practice that prepares them (Bainbridge 1983). Teams must keep the skill on purpose: reading the audit’s findings in the code, tracing incidents by hand, rotating who does it.
Limits of the model. It is linear and treats defects as independent. It does not weight defects by harm, so if reviewers mainly catch severe ones it is biased against the gate; the irreversible cases, which keep their gate, are meant to cover the worst. It counts the audit as an hour of reading, ignoring its compute cost and false alarms. It holds d constant, although reviewers tire and large changes get shallower reviews, and it ignores what reviewers learn. The thin gate’s catch rate is assumed equal to a reviewer’s, not measured. The parameters describe one team at one rate: the direction of the result holds wherever Equation 3 holds, not its magnitude. Finally, the paper assumes writing code is no longer the bottleneck, and the evidence on how much AI speeds up experienced developers is mixed (Becker et al. 2025).

title: Stop Reviewing Pull Requests
text:
9. Conclusion
The pull request review was the right control while late defects were expensive and a person’s reading was the main check. With agentic coding, rules run inside every session, most defects are cheap to fix the next day, and the one step that has not become faster is the person reading the diff.
What keeps a codebase healthy is how quickly defects are found and how cheaply they are undone, not whether someone looked at each change before it merged. Where harm cannot be undone, a person still decides, late and briefly, at the point of no return: the gate guards the act, not the code. Where a machine cannot see, the team should measure that before it lets go.
This means giving up control of each change. In return, we can simplify our processes instead of adding layers to protect a kind of control that, in the past, was the only kind available. Approve what you cannot undo. Watch everything else.

Read next · Review the Intent, Not the Diff How the Claude Code team solved code review, and the one thing I would let go of.


The views in this paper are my own and do not describe any product or plan of my employer.
